rationale: The signal the whole product rests on. Kivi inserted one form, the user replaced it with a phonetically close one in the same field. That pair, and nothing else, is what 'fix it once' means.

The filter that keeps the memory clean. The user rewrote the sentence; they did not correct a word. Without a phonetic gate on the learner, every stylistic edit becomes a spurious lexeme and the store fills with noise within a day.

observation.after: Please ask Aadith when he has a moment to review it

rationale: A near-miss for the same filter: a short edit that is nevertheless a substitution of meaning, not of spelling. Phonetic distance is the discriminator, not edit length.
An explicit dictionary add is the user speaking directly. It becomes usable immediately - requiring repetition here would be user-hostile and would make the demo feel broken.

Two identical corrections in the same scope promote a lexeme from PROPOSED to ACTIVE. The threshold of two is a claim about the product, and the fix-it-once curve in the report is what has to justify it.

The same two corrections spread across two different apps. Evidence is scope-AGNOSTIC for the purpose of believing a term: a person who fixed their colleague's name once in Slack and once in Mail has fixed it twice, and telling them those were two separate pieces of evidence is an implementation detail leaking into the product. So the lexeme activates. Scope still governs where a term APPLIES - B4-001 asserts that a Slack handle is refused inside Mail - it just no longer fragments the evidence for whether the term is believed at all. This case was rewritten when D-010 was settled; it previously asserted the conservative behaviour.
A revert is evidence, not an error. It enters the same Beta posterior as a supporting observation, with a heavier weight, so confidence falls without the lexeme disappearing.

Two reverts in the same scope create a suppression guard rather than deleting the lexeme, because the term is still real - it is this context the user does not want it in. Produces the state that B8-001 then tests.
A spoken instruction about a term, not a correction of one. It sets the canonical form and a standing instruction in a single step and carries declared-level weight.

observation.after: always write it Aadith with two a's

rationale: A term read from surrounding on-screen text. Broad and cheap but unverified - the user never confirmed anything - so it can only ever reach PROPOSED on its own. This is where an over-eager implementation starts inventing memories.

observation.surrounding_text: invoice from Kshatriya Systems dated 12 January

rationale: The user renames a canonical form. A tombstone with reason 'supersession' preserves the old match surfaces, so the previous spelling still resolves to the new lexeme instead of being re-learned from zero.
An edit that changes only case is real evidence about how the user writes a term, but it must not create a second lexeme for the same word. Attaches as a styling variant to the existing entry.

An explicit forget. The lexeme is tombstoned rather than dropped, so a later sighting of the same form does not silently recreate what the user deleted - which would read as the product ignoring them.
Learning is off for this lexeme. The correction is still applied at runtime, but no new variant is recorded - the two behaviours are separately controllable and this case pins that down.

Decay with no new evidence. An ACTIVE lexeme falls to DORMANT purely through the passage of time, with the clock pinned so the result is identical on any day the suite is run. Produces the state A11-001 and B10-001 depend on.
